KEY MESSAGE 1...A few rain showers today through tonight across the 
North Country, dry and warmer elsewhere.

Another fast moving mid level shortwave and associated surface low 
will cross southern Quebec today, reaching New England this evening. 
The southern extent of DPVA and height falls will brush northern NY 
today. Modest lake induced instability will combine with the 
synoptic scale forcing to produce a few light showers across the 
North Country and Saint Lawrence Valley today into this evening. The 
best shower coverage will be across the Tug Hill Plateau and western 
Adirondacks with an added boost of upslope flow. A few leftover 
showers this evening will end overnight as synoptic scale moisture 
and forcing depart, and a weak ridge axis builds into the eastern 
Great Lakes.

Today will be the warmest day of the week, with highs reaching the 
upper 50s to lower 60s across the lower elevations of Western and 
Central NY, with low to mid 50s for higher terrain and the North 
Country. It will become quite breezy again as a belt of 30 to 40 
knot flow in the boundary layer crosses the eastern Great Lakes. 
This will partially mix to the surface from mid morning through mid 
afternoon, with gusts in the 25 to 35 mph range areawide.

Wednesday will be mainly dry for most of the day with increasing 
clouds ahead of the next system. Some light rain may develop towards 
evening across Western NY.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Unsettled and colder weather will return Wednesday 
night through the end of the week, with some minor wet snow 
potential mainly across higher terrain.

Bottom line up front. While the weather will be chilly and
unsettled Thursday through Saturday, latest model and ensemble
data suggests minimal winter weather impacts through the period.

The longwave pattern will amplify Thursday through Friday with a 
sharp ridge over the Rockies forcing a deep trough and broad closed 
low to become established over the eastern CONUS and southeastern 
Canada. At the surface, an initial low will reach the Ohio Valley 
Wednesday night, then give way to secondary coastal cyclogenesis off 
the Mid Atlantic coast by Thursday. An elongated surface low, or 
possibly a series of individual low centers will then move northeast 
and offshore of New England Thursday night through Saturday before 
reaching the Canadian Maritimes Saturday night.

Large scale forcing will increase Wednesday night through Thursday 
as the closed low takes shape upstream, with significant height 
falls spreading east across the Great Lakes. This will combine with 
frontogenesis and deformation north of the initial low track to 
bring periods of light rain Wednesday night through Thursday across 
the region. Precip type will stay all rain through Thursday evening, 
with the possible exception of the highest terrain of the North 
Country.

Thursday night through Saturday, cold air will deepen across the 
eastern Great Lakes as the surface low strengthens off the New 
England coast, and the mid level closed low matures overhead. The 
stronger synoptic scale forcing will focus along the New England 
coast and well east of our area, leaving a weakly forced moist 
northerly flow regime across the eastern Great Lakes. Abundant wrap 
around moisture will combine with lake induced instability and north 
to northeast flow to produce occasional showers through the period, 
with the best coverage across higher terrain from upslope 
enhancement.

The airmass will grow cold enough to allow the rain to mix with and 
change to wet snow across higher terrain Thursday night through 
Friday. The coldest air aloft will then arrive Friday night through 
Saturday, when lower elevations will have the best chance of a mix 
or change to wet snow. The lack of stronger synoptic scale forcing 
and short fetch northerly flow will likely keep precipitation rates 
light, and light wet snow falling on warm ground will struggle to 
accumulate. 

The latest probabilistic forecasts from the full ensemble suite of 
the NBM and LREF Grand Ensemble suggest a high likelihood of very 
minor accumulations across higher terrain Friday through Saturday, 
but minimal chance of anything more than very minor impacts. 
Ensemble data suggests no accumulation for lower elevations 
including the main population centers of the region. 

This system will gradually pull away Sunday through Monday with a 
return to dry weather early next week. Cool temperatures will 
persist for a few days before a warming trend develops by the middle 
of next week.
